newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire welcomes U.S. warning, rebels push west.
newsitem.headline: Zaire welcomes U.S. warning, rebels push west.

text.p: Zaire, which has repeatedly accused Rwanda and Uganda of invading to back Tutsi-led rebels in the east, has welcomed a U.S. call for neighbouring countries to stay out of the civil war.

But as the United States, France and Belgium all expressed concern at a possible escalation of the revolt into a wider regional conflict, rebel forces pushed west, capturing the town of Shabunda and extending the area under their control.

The Zairean Defence Ministry, in a statement issued on Thursday, expressed "satisfaction" at Wednesday's U.S. call that Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi respect Kinshasa's territorial integrity and stay out of the fighting.
Zairean defence officials acknowledged the fall of Shabunda on Wednesday but played down the impact of the rebel advance, saying they had had only a few soldiers in the area.
They have acknowledged a rebel thrust into mineral-rich Shaba province in the south and the fall of Kalemie there.
But they hotly denied rebel claims to be near Lubutu on the road to Kisangani, headquarters for the army counter-offensive launched on January 20, and Isoro to the north east.

Aid workers caring for over 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees outside in Lubutu, around 200 km (125 miles) from Kisangani, told Reuters that 70 wounded soldiers had been brought into a hospital in the town.
They reported some refugees leaving Amisi, about 80 km (50 miles) further down the road to the rebel-held east. Other sources reported fighting close to a refugee camp there.
Zairean officials said the refugees had been panicked by rumours. "They are fleeing because of rumours," one said.
The U.N. World Food Programme had contingency plans to evacuate staff from Lubutu and nearby Tingi Tingi refugee camp if it proved necessary.
"We are keeping a plane on standby at Kisangani to evacuate aid workers from Lubutu should the situation deteriorate," Brenda Barton of the WFP told Reuters.
Zaire's army headquarters, meanwhile, issued a statement asking what had happened to military equipment it said had been taken to Uganda for use by a planned international force.
The plan fell apart after over 500,000 Hutus trekked home to Rwanda at the end of last year when the rebels attacked hardliners in their midst in their camps in the east.

But relief officials have expressed increasing concern at the plight of several hundred thousand Hutus trapped by the fighting after fleeing west in December with the hardliners, who were blamed for the 1994 genocide of Tutsis in Rwanda.
The rebels say their thrusts on several fronts have stopped the army counter-offensive in its tracks and they have given President Mobutu Sese Seko until February 21 to stand down.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, a veteran Mobutu foe, told 5,000 newly trained recruits in Goma on Thursday that his forces now controlled a large slice of territory along the borders with Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda.
"You and I have a duty to remove Mobutu and his corrupt and rotten system and relegate them to the dustbins of history," he said.
The rebels launched their offensive in October accusing the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and planning to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.
Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 but bowed to pressure for democratic reform in 1990, was expected back in Kinshasa by the weekend after medical tests in Europe following prostate surgery in August.
On the way, he has visited Morocco which sent troops to help him crush rebellions in Shaba in the 1970s.
